papers.title: Self-Consistent Neural Control: Learning Trajectories for Implicit Equilibrium
papers.abstract: One big challenge in physical AI is interacting with systems whose states are defined by implicit equilibrium. Learning in these systems is difficult because their responses can be multistable, path-dependent, and sensitive over long horizons. Adjoint learning provides an efficient way to optimize trajectories without unrolling iterative equilibrium solvers, but its gradient relies on the frozen-tangent approximation, which neglects higher-order sensitivity terms and can become inaccurate when the local equilibrium varies rapidly. In this work, we introduce Self-Consistent Neural Control (SCNC), optimizing trajectories along which sensitivity variations are explicitly controlled. We derive a mathematical bound on the resulting gradient error and develop a practical finite-difference approximation. We validate the framework on deformable objects, which are representative of implicit equilibrium systems, ranging from simple quadratic energy models such as elastic rods to complex systems including thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures. Compared with the adjoint learning and the gradient-free iCEM baselines, SCNC achieves faster convergence and more stable optimization by reducing switching to undesirable equilibrium branches, doubling the stable optimization rate over adjoint learning 83.3% vs. 41.7% and reducing the average loss by more than 1.5 orders of magnitude on thin-walled tubes, where sensitivity variations are pronounced.

papers.title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
papers.abstract: Simulation benchmarks are the standard way to compare robot policies, but each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention, and evaluation is slow: 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU take 359.7 minutes. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluator shows that simulation occupies CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. RoboScope Kit wraps each model once in a Python class called a Policy, and each benchmark once in an adapter around the benchmark's own evaluator, so the benchmark's rules and scoring stay unchanged. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both from measured probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances; runtime optimization renders only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one 48 GiB RTX 4090, the concurrency search selects twelve simulator workers sharing three Policy replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45$\times$ faster than the official StarVLA evaluation with equivalent success rates, 2.78$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 1.52$\times$ faster than vla-eval at its tuned configuration. With CUDA MPS, which lets the replicas run their kernels concurrently, the search selects sixteen workers sharing four replicas, 6.16$\times$ faster than StarVLA, 3.85$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 2.10$\times$ faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Shape Servoing of Deformable Objects-Part II: Advanced Concepts
papers.abstract: In robotics, shape control, or shape servoing, refers to the automatic manipulation of a deformable object toward a desired shape. This article is the second of a two-part tutorial on data-driven, Jacobian-based shape control, in which the deformation Jacobian, a local model of how robot motion changes the measured shape, is estimated from measurements. Part I built the shape-servoing loop and derived a local stability condition. This paper starts by using the singular value decomposition of the deformation Jacobian to identify shape changes that can be produced by small robot motions, those that require large robot motions, and those that are locally unavailable. It then analyses how the choice of shape features determines how the controller regulates the object's shape and, therefore, how much the object deforms on its way to the target. It then describes three ways in which the shape control loop can fail: loss of controllability, loss of observability, and occurrence of mechanical instabilities. It closes with shape-control extensions to time-varying targets, secondary tasks, and three-dimensional objects.

papers.title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data
papers.abstract: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, this https URL . Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.

papers.title: Robot-Matched Soft Fingers for UMI Data Collection: Lessons from 100 Hours of Pick and Place
papers.abstract: Training robot policies for multi-task pick and place requires demonstrations on many objects, which handheld Universal Manipulation Interfaces (UMIs) can collect quickly and cheaply. However, existing UMIs depend on external base stations, use rigid fingers that give no signal about contact forces, or use parallel-jaw fingers that limit grip strength. We present a battery-powered handheld interface, built on YUBI, whose soft, angled fingers wrap around objects, deform visibly under load as a visual proxy for force, and match the grippers of the robot. With it, we collect a 99.7-hour dataset over 53 objects, train $\pi_{0.5}$ policies on 49 of them, and hold out the other 4 as unseen objects. We find that a top camera raises success by 13 points even when only about half of the data includes it, and that mid-training on our multi-task data raises success after fine-tuning on unseen objects from 35% to 57%. papers.title: DreamX: Video Diffusion Model is a Universal Latent Action Learner
papers.abstract: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model's rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by $\boldsymbol{300\times}$ ($\boldsymbol{1{,}200 \rightarrow 4}$ tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model's generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.

papers.title: Visibility-Aware Reference Generation for Benchmarking Visual 3D Reconstruction in Vegetation-Rich Environments
papers.abstract: Reliable evaluation of visual 3D reconstruction and depth estimation in vegetation-rich outdoor environments is limited by the scarcity of geometric ground-truth data and the cost of complete scanner surveys. We present a LiDARbased reference-generation pipeline for evaluating the zero-shot performance of feed-forward visual-geometry models alongside conventional structure-from-motion (SfM) methods. The pipeline reuses camera images, LiDAR scans, and reference poses from existing multi-sensor localization datasets to generate per-view depth maps and visible reference point clouds. To address visibility errors in accumulated LiDAR scans, we introduce the LargeDepth-Gap Visibility Score (LDGVS) for point-wise visibility filtering and automatic scale selection in Hidden Point Removal(HPR). Experiments on TartanAirV2 and TartanGround show that, compared with Poisson surface reconstruction, which is an approach suited to completed scan surveys, the combined HPR and LDGVS filtering retains approximately three times the point density at comparable absolute relative error. We also apply the pipeline to the BotanicGarden dataset to systematically compare depth estimation and 3D reconstruction methods. Feedforward methods produce dense depth predictions efficiently, but their 3D reconstructions can contain duplicated structures. Conventional SfM generally produces more coherent geometry, but its reconstructions remain sparse and more prone to failure in challenging vegetated scenes. The benchmark toolkit and datasets will be released.

papers.title: PadLoc: Training-Free Floor-Plan Localization by Sparse Geometric Matching
papers.abstract: We propose PadLoc, a training-free localization back-end that places a moving sensor within a known floor plan. Floor plans are cheap, persistent, and robust to appearance change, but recent learned-depth methods localize against them by filtering per-frame depth through dense $(x,y,\theta)$ pose grids. PadLoc keeps the swappable depth front-end and replaces the dense grid back-end with sparse geometric matching: dominant wall orientations define a small pose-candidate set, masked normalized cross-correlation scores observed free space against the plan, and a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter plus consensus readout decodes the trajectory. Holding each competitor's depth fixed, PadLoc matches or beats UnLoc's forward filter and the F3Loc filter at every Gibson trajectory length, and UnLoc's offline refinement from $T=35$ on; it exceeds Z-FLoc's published results with a shared MapAnything front-end. On Bonn LiLocBench, PadLoc improves pooled SR@1m over UnLoc by 23-32 pp under wheel odometry and 35-43 pp with ground-truth motion; with full-FOV LiDAR plus wheel odometry the same readout reaches 100% SR@1m at 9-10 cm median error on the static sequence. On the Hilti-Trimble Localization Challenge PadLoc localizes a camera-only fisheye rig on construction floors hundreds of metres across at 0.90-0.98 online SR@2m on three of five sessions; adding learned wall isolation, applied to every session, covers all five at 0.67-0.92 with the localizer unchanged throughout. PadLoc thus matches or outperforms dense grid back-ends while preserving sensor modularity and a compact state that does not grow with trajectory length.

papers.title: Sparse Anchors for Visual Multi-Session Registration in Changing Environments
papers.abstract: Repeated robotic monitoring requires localization across visits to the same environment, even if the environment changes. Such changes can substantially reduce persistent visual content, and repetitive structures can lead to incorrect cross-session correspondences. In this paper, we address visual multi-session registration of a new data recording (the query session) to a previously reconstructed reference map. Under substantial visual and structural changes, cross-session localization may be possible only for parts of the trajectory. In our approach, we therefore rely on a sparse set of reliable absolute pose constraints and combine them with within-session relative-pose information to register the complete trajectory to the reference map. We first estimate absolute alignment hypotheses through visual place recognition, local feature matching, and geometric verification. We then use sequence consensus to reject hypotheses that are inconsistent with a common query-to-reference alignment and retain the remaining poses as absolute anchors. These anchors are refined through featuremetric alignment against a Gaussian feature field and combined with within-session relative-pose constraints in a robust pose-graph optimization. We evaluate our approach on 15 cross-session experiments from the challenging HILTI26 construction-site dataset, covering substantial scene changes and difficult-to-match environments. Our method achieves 94.4% recall within 1m and 100.0% within 5m, outperforming independent image localization, which peaks at 65.3% and 70.7%, respectively, as well as direct registration of independently reconstructed Structure-from-Motion geometry. Our results show that sparse, reliable absolute anchors can provide accurate and complete trajectory registration even when reliable cross-session correspondences are available only for part of the query session.

papers.title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
papers.abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.

papers.title: For You, Not for Everyone: Bystander-Aware Delivery of Critical Feedback in Robot Tutoring
papers.abstract: Robots in shared settings may expose information intended for an individual user to nearby bystanders. Robot tutoring makes this concern particularly salient: critical feedback is directed at an individual learner, yet bystanders may overhear or see it. To address this, we compared context-invariant and context-adaptive robot behaviors in a between-subjects study with 40 participants. Following an initial phase without a bystander, a bystander entered the setting. Participants then received two scripted critical feedback messages concerning their pronunciation and handwriting, independent of their actual performance. With the context-invariant behavior, the robot tutor delivered both messages aloud. With the context-adaptive behavior, the robot tutor scanned for the bystander, turned its body and display away after detecting them, gave a spoken attention cue, and presented the same feedback messages silently on its display. Participants rated the robot tutor higher in perceived privacy awareness and perceived social competence in the context-adaptive condition than in the context-invariant condition, while evidence for reduced experienced embarrassment was inconclusive. These findings inform the design and evaluation of robots that respond to bystander presence by adapting how they communicate potentially sensitive information.

papers.title: iMED: A Multi-Endoscope Dataset for Surgical 3D Perception
papers.abstract: We introduce iMED, the first synchronized multi-endoscope dataset for robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS), designed to address a fundamental limitation in surgical vision benchmarking: the absence of independent held-out viewpoints. Existing surgical datasets capture single-trajectory sequences from a single endoscope, making it impossible to distinguish geometric generalization from photometric interpolation along a narrow forward-facing path. iMED provides 340 sequences ~170K synchronized timepoints with 4 views per timepoint) recorded simultaneously from two independent stereo endoscopes across ex vivo, postmortem, and live surgical settings, spanning 14 specimens with diverse anatomical regions and motion regimes. The dataset includes calibrated camera intrinsics, ArUco-based frame-wise pose estimates with uncertainty quantification, instrument segmentation masks, and rich clinical metadata. Using a train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another evaluation protocol, we benchmark 23 state-of-the-art methods across rigid and deformable novel view synthesis, pose estimation, feature matching, and monocular depth estimation. Our experiments show that methods relying primarily on photometric supervision degrade substantially under this held-out-endoscope setting, while methods with explicit geometric regularization are more robust across views in our benchmark. Notably, large-scale foundation models transfer surprisingly well to surgical imagery, often outperforming domain-specific models, suggesting pitfalls in current fine-tuning protocols. iMED establishes a new evaluation protocol for geometric generalization in surgical vision.

papers.title: Cycle WAM: Coupling Action and Video through Cycle Consistency
papers.abstract: Recent advances in video modeling have driven substantial progress in world action models (WAMs). Existing approaches exploit pretrained video priors by decoding actions from latent representations or inferring them from generated videos. The underlying link is causal: robot actions produce changes in the scene, and video observations of these changes provide evidence for inferring the actions that produced them. However, existing training formulations do not by themselves ensure that actions and their predicted visual consequences are consistent, potentially limiting the use of pretrained capabilities. We treat video and action as paired modalities linked by this causal relationship and learn their correspondence through a unified training framework designed to better exploit pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM first augments video-action co-training with bidirectional conversion to reinforce cross-modal correspondence and recover forward and inverse dynamics. It then introduces a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective to further couple the two mappings. The resulting model supports both forward and inverse dynamics, with the potential to improve performance through more effective use of pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID. Comparisons with UWM characterize its inverse-dynamics performance and show sharper visual detail in the displayed forward-dynamics predictions.

papers.title: Just Between Us? Exploring a Wearable-Mediated Channel for Discreet Human-Agent Interaction in a Shared Game Setting
papers.abstract: In shared settings, social robots may need to exchange information with an individual while limiting co-present others' access to or interpretation of that information. Publicly observable speech and gestures may not adequately support such exchanges. We investigate a wearable-mediated channel for discreet interaction that combines in-ear audio messages with deliberate rightward head tilts as responses. To examine its feasibility and participants' experiences, we studied 20 pairs (40 participants) playing a card game with a screen-based conversational agent representing a social robot, controlled by a researcher in a Wizard-of-Oz setup. Each pair played with and without the channel. One participant wore the device (the wearer), while the other (the non-wearer) was informed about the channel after gameplay. The channel conveyed information that could help the wearer or robot character select an opponent they could defeat. The information exchange and subsequent opponent selection occurred as intended in 39 of 40 channel-mediated turns. Wearers reported low perceived pressure/tension in both conditions, with no statistically significant difference between conditions, and favorable usability immediately after use. Retrospective interviews, however, revealed varied accounts of noticing the interaction among non-wearers and contrasting perceptions of teamwork and unfairness. These findings support the feasibility of wearable-mediated exchanges within this game and identify awareness and fairness as considerations for future designs.

papers.title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code ( this https URL ), the trained policy (72.6 MB, this https URL ) and the full benchmark dataset are public.

papers.title: ReSMap: Recasting Satellite Priors for Robust and Accurate Online HD Map Construction
papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in camera-based online HD map construction, these systems remain susceptible to sensor failures due to their reliance on onboard cameras. In contrast, satellite images remain available independently of real-time sensing conditions as they are cached offline. Existing methods utilizing satellite images, however, primarily leverage them under nominal conditions, without explicitly addressing them as redundancy when a sensor degrades. To address this gap, we propose ReSMap, a redundancy-aware camera-satellite fusion framework for robust online HD map construction. Our framework explicitly leverages satellite images as a complementary source to improve robustness against camera failures. A Predict-then-Fuse (PTF) module fuses camera and satellite BEV features by using each branch's own prediction confidence as a per-pixel reliability weight, with no learned router. An Object-Centric Cooperative Multi-modal Query (OCMQ) decoder then extends this per-modality separation to the query level: each modality cross-attends only to its own BEV, and per-modality updates are merged through a learned per-token gate. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on nuScenes across all splits and range settings. More importantly, it also sets the new state-of-the-art under camera-failure scenarios, demonstrating that satellite images serve not only as a strong prior but as practical redundancy for robust online HD mapping.

papers.title: Computing Invariant Reachable Sets through Sum-of-Squares Programming
papers.abstract: Funnels, time-varying invariant sets around nominal trajectories, certify that a closed-loop system tracks its plan, and can be composed into verified motion plans. Their computation by sum-of-squares (SOS) programming is well established in formulation but not in practice: the result depends on implementation choices such as the initial guess, Lyapunov function normalization, and termination rule, which the literature documents only briefly. This paper presents a self-contained treatment of SOS-based funnel computation, implemented in the open-source package computeSOSFunnels. We propose a minimum-volume formulation with inlet and outlet constraints under which funnels with coinciding nominal endpoints compose by construction. Numerical experiments on a unicycle, with timing studies on a cart-pole and a 12-state quadrotor, characterize the pipeline: infeasible initial guesses are partly decidable before solving, the certificate shows no violations among 39,000 boundary samples per funnel under the true dynamics, and constructing the semidefinite program, not solving it, dominates computation time.

papers.title: Say the Same, Act Differently: Diagnosing and Steering Text-Action Divergence in Reasoning VLAs
papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models pair physical control with natural-language rationales that supervisors can read to monitor embodied safety. Prior attacks on VLA reasoning corrupt the rationale itself and leave visible evidence in the text. We show that visual perturbations can instead alter the physical action while keeping the generated rationale word-for-word identical. At the shared text/action interface of Alpamayo for driving and InstructVLA for manipulation, our text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic shows that the locally most action-sensitive direction is nearly orthogonal to the active text-loss gradients, with 1.87% and 5.28% norm overlap. At equal hidden-state perturbation norms across both models, interventions along this text-neutral residual shift actions 4.64x to 47.8x more than text-gradient perturbations, whereas text-gradient perturbations induce 21.2x to 277x more text drift. Steering visual perturbations along this direction reaches the same decoupling from the image. Across 154 obstacle-annotated driving scenes in Alpamayo, TNAS-guided attacks induce a new collision under a word-for-word identical rationale in 52.6% of scenes under full-image perturbations and 35.1% under a localized forward-camera patch, compared with 4.55% for unguided action attacks. Relative to a text-preserving baseline, TNAS guidance raises exact rationale preservation from 83.0% to 89.5% and cuts teacher-forced text drift by 68.4% at a comparable collision rate. In InstructVLA, TNAS guidance cuts text drift by 40.5% and preserves the exact response on 85.0% of examples alongside a 1.73-unit action-chunk shift. An unchanged rationale therefore cannot certify a safe action, so monitors for reasoning VLAs must verify the predicted action channel directly.

papers.title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection
papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.

papers.title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection
papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.

papers.title: te-comp: A Complete MLIR Compiler Generating Self-Contained C Inference Engines for MCUs
papers.abstract: Deploying deep learning on microcontrollers (MCUs) requires fitting both the model weights and runtime activations within tens to hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM and Flash. Existing approaches either use an interpreter with a pre-written kernel library or combine a Python code generator with hand-written C kernels. This incurs dispatch overhead and requires framework dependencies. None produces self-contained, dependency-free C code specialized to a given model. In this paper, we present te-comp, the first complete MLIR-based compiler that takes a standard model in .tflite or .safetensors format and emits all C source files needed for deployment: the inference engine (kernels, weight arrays, memory layout) and the RTOS integration layer with zero runtime dependencies. On 10 MCUNet CNN benchmarks, te-comp outperforms MCUNet TinyEngine by using 38% less SRAM (up to 5.9$\times$) and 15% less Flash, while generating complete C code rather than linking a pre-written kernel library. To demonstrate, we use te-comp to compile an 8.3M-parameter GPT-Neo transformer (TinyStories-v2) and deploy it on a single-core Cortex-M7 at 160MHz. The full firmware uses 249KB of 512KB SRAM and 3.62MB of 4MB Flash and achieves approximately 1 token/s interactive text generation via Q4_0 weight quantization, a stateful int4 KV cache, and vocabulary pruning -- a capability no existing MCU inference framework supports.

executive_summary: WayTrace converts web-map directions into atomic language commands with a vision-language orchestrator, predicts per-command image-space paths from over one million automatically labeled street-level images, and tracks them via a reinforcement learning policy; in long-range simulated missions it remains robust under GNSS noise with ~10× fewer crosswalk/sidewalk violations than point-goal baselines, and on a wheeled-legged robot it completes urban, rural-trail, and campus routes up to 1.37 km at ~1.1 m/s, negotiating crosswalks, stairs, and construction sites.

institution_matches.title: WayTrace: A Map-to-Language-to-Trace Hierarchy for Embodied Urban Navigation
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes WayTrace, a hierarchical navigation system that converts web-map turn-by-turn directions into atomic language commands using an orchestrator vision-language model, predicts per-command image-space paths with a trace predictor trained on over one million automatically labeled street-level images, and tracks these paths using a reinforcement learning policy. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace maintains robustness to GNSS noise and incurs roughly ten times fewer crosswalk and sidewalk violations than point-goal navigation baselines, which degrade sharply under the same conditions. On a wheeled-legged robot in real-world tests, WayTrace completes urban, rural-trail, and campus navigation missions up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s, successfully handling crosswalks, staircases, and construction sites.

institution_matches.title: Physical Experience Builds Continual Spatial World Models
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces a continual spatial world modeling framework in a dynamic maze that separates episodic spatial changes from continuous action consequences, combining Cross-episode Spatial Change Memory for learning relations among transformations with state-action-outcome experience for refining motion predictions. Experiments show that structured repeated physical experience progressively reduces the need for future route corrections, enables transfer to spatial transitions not seen during learning, and that this advantage disappears when past environmental changes carry no information about future ones. Continuous navigation and physical tests demonstrate that predictive memory updates behavior when prior decisions become invalid, that correct topological knowledge alone does not guarantee accurate action prediction, and that accumulating physical experience reduces this mismatch within the modeled dynamics.

institution_matches.title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
institution_matches.overview: The paper presents PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision inverse kinematics that updates joint-position references from pose feedback, tracks accumulated reference offsets relative to measured joints, and uses two-scale pose errors with error-dependent action gains plus progress-and-dwell rewards to both reach and maintain a desired tolerance. In simulation, a PPO-trained PolicyIK policy keeps mean end-effector errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2° on 93.5% of held-out tasks with a single attempt, and a deployment protocol increases this success rate to 98.9%. Trained directly on a physical robot arm with off-policy RL, PolicyIK attains higher reaching and holding success than four classical IK controllers under equal time budgets, and in simulated pick-and-place it executes the end-effector commands of the π₀.₅ VLA policy with 95.7% success.

institution_matches.title: Online Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability Onboard the Robot Control Loop: A Real-Time GPU Solver for Safety-Critical Autonomy
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces a CUDA-based implementation of the canonical WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs level-set solver for 2D–4D dynamics, enabling Hamilton-Jacobi reachability to run inside a robot’s control loop as a real-time safety layer. On a single NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada GPU in FP32, the solver computes the 3D Air3D BRT at 112 Hz, a 4D pursuit–evasion BRT at 61 Hz, and a 2D wind-affected drifter BRT at 74–147 Hz, achieving roughly 5.9–17.5× speedup over the JAX hj_reachability implementation and 1.7–16× over a matched reimplementation, while in FP64 it agrees with hj_reachability on eight benchmarks and reproduces Mitchell’s Air3D BRT cell count within 0.04% at 2.0–4.6× speedup. On an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, the solver computes Air3D at 66 Hz (N=41) and the 2D drifter at 54 Hz, 3.8–8.9× faster than hj_reachability, and an in-kernel label-propagation extension recovers K-agent capture-basin Voronoi tessellations from a single combined solve, running at 4.0 ms per tick in a closed-loop wildfire-response simulation of six quadcopters under time-varying, non-uniform wind.

institution_matches.title: Sparse Anchors for Visual Multi-Session Registration in Changing Environments
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes a multi-session visual registration method that uses a sparse set of reliable absolute pose constraints (“anchors”) obtained from visual place recognition, feature matching, geometric verification, and sequence consensus, combined with within-session relative-pose constraints in a robust pose-graph optimization, to register a query trajectory to a reference map under substantial scene changes. Absolute pose hypotheses are refined via featuremetric alignment against a Gaussian feature field, and inconsistent hypotheses are rejected through sequence consensus to retain only anchors that support a common query-to-reference alignment. On 15 cross-session experiments from the HILTI26 construction-site dataset, the method achieves 94.4% recall within 1 m and 100.0% within 5 m, outperforming independent image localization (65.3% and 70.7%) and direct registration of independently reconstructed SfM geometry, indicating that sparse reliable anchors can yield accurate and complete trajectory registration even when cross-session correspondences exist only along parts of the query path.

institution_matches.title: Self-Consistent Neural Control: Learning Trajectories for Implicit Equilibrium
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces Self-Consistent Neural Control (SCNC), a trajectory optimization framework for systems with implicitly defined equilibria that explicitly controls sensitivity variations along trajectories, derives a bound on the resulting gradient error, and implements a practical finite-difference approximation to improve learning beyond the frozen-tangent adjoint approximation. Validated on deformable-object systems ranging from quadratic energy models (elastic rods) to complex thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures, SCNC achieves faster and more stable optimization than adjoint learning and the gradient-free iCEM baseline by reducing switching to undesirable equilibrium branches. On thin-walled tubes, where sensitivity variations are pronounced, SCNC doubles the stable optimization rate compared to adjoint learning (83.3% vs. 41.7%) and reduces average loss by more than 1.5 orders of magnitude.

institution_matches.title: Hybrid Particle-Voxel Dynamics for Multimodal 3D World Simulation
institution_matches.overview: The paper presents 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world model that uses a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder to compress point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents and an action-conditioned latent dynamics model to jointly predict future geometry, appearance, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. The shared 3D latent representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and integration of spatially aligned tactile signals, enabling interactive long-horizon multimodal prediction at 50 Hz in experiments. Using large datasets of diverse objects, the model supports scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation with multi-view and tactile observations, and demonstrates model-based planning on unseen objects and robot configurations, highlighting hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a basis for multimodal 3D world simulation.

institution_matches.title: HiLo-WAM: Decoupling Long-Horizon Task Evolution and Local Dynamics in World Action Models
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes HiLo-WAM, a world action model architecture that decouples long-horizon task evolution from local visual dynamics via two visual streams—a sparse long-horizon stream for historical context and future evolution, and a dense short-horizon stream for local robot–object interactions—implemented within a dual-DiT model where actions are guided by structured cross-stream attention. HiLo-WAM introduces progressive inference with stream-wise partial denoising, joint denoising, and dynamic skipping to reduce computation while leveraging the complementary temporal scales of the two streams. Experiments show that HiLo-WAM attains a 93.70% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon manipulation tasks, with robust in-domain and out-of-distribution performance on the Fourier GR-3 robot, and that progressive inference yields a 2.93× speedup while further improving performance; ablations confirm the importance of both long-horizon and local dynamics streams and appropriate temporal-scale balancing.

institution_matches.title: Should the Action Expert Train the VLM? Action-Token Supervision and Gradient Routing in Mixture-of-Transformer VLAs
institution_matches.overview: The paper studies training recipes for mixture-of-transformer vision-language-action models that pair a pre-trained VLM with a flow-matching action expert, independently varying whether expert losses backpropagate into the VLM (coupling vs. insulation) and whether the VLM is supervised to predict discrete action tokens encoding target actions. In open-loop driving, when action-token supervision is present, gradient insulation performs competitively with coupling, but without action tokens, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25% compared to insulation. When both components are trained jointly from scratch, coupling the expert’s gradients into the VLM improves closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and about 40% without it, and similarly boosts robot manipulation performance under both conditions, indicating that the benefit of insulating the VLM depends strongly on action supervision and evaluation setting.

institution_matches.title: GSBR: Geometric Support Behavior Regularization for Online RL
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), an online reinforcement learning regularizer that penalizes actions based on their distance to the support of a pretrained base policy, imposing no penalty within the estimated support while allowing smooth, value-driven exploration outside it; the distance is estimated from finite samples of the base policy, requiring only sample access. By regularizing toward the geometric support rather than the full base-policy distribution, GSBR encourages the RL actor to focus on high-value modes and avoids forbidding beneficial actions that lie just outside the base policy’s support, addressing the over-restrictiveness of behavioral cloning regularizers and hard support constraints. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR improves average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success and about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method.

topic_matches.title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes AIRoA-0 (A-0), a bimanual manipulation system trained solely on 16,151 hours of handheld YUBI-gripper demonstrations (no robot data, teleoperation, RL, or on-robot corrections), that uses only wrist cameras and a continuous action stream to perform long-horizon tasks across multiple robot embodiments. In real-robot evaluations across ten manipulation tasks at a site disjoint from the handheld data collection locations, A-0 achieves an average success rate of 78%, substantially outperforming the strongest of four post-trained vision-language-action baselines, which attains 27% success on the same task demonstrations. The system includes mechanisms to learn task-relevant wrist-view regions, infer task stage, and operate on multiple robots that mount the YUBI gripper (e.g., bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm, UR), and the authors release what they state is the largest open handheld-gripper demonstration dataset with task and subtask instructions, along with pretrained weights and a post-training recipe.

topic_matches.title: A Practical Causal Framework for Autonomous Mobile Robots: From Simulation to Real-World Human Environments
topic_matches.institution: National Research Council of Italy; University of Padua
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes a causal inference framework for autonomous mobile robots that transfers high-level causal structures learned in simulation to real-world human environments, adapting to real conditions by updating only the causal model parameters using a limited set of real-world observations. topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces FEIJOA, a language-model-based agent for mobile manipulation that grounds instructions at test time by iteratively querying a grounding tool over RGB-D scans, inspecting candidate objects/locations, refining queries, and using an embodiment-aware harness to check skill preconditions, sample reachable base poses, and verify execution effects. topic_matches.title: ActOR: Ambient AI-Based Agentic Orchestration for Humanoid Autonomy in Operating Rooms
topic_matches.institution: Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions; Johns Hopkins University
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes ActOR, an ambient AI-based orchestration framework that fuses a wall-mounted camera with a humanoid’s head camera into an object-level digital twin, over which a large language model agent plans multi-step locomotion and manipulation in operating rooms using pre-programmed skills and closed-loop feedback from digital twin updates and execution outcomes. topic_matches.title: ReflexArc: Bottom-Up Integration of Instantaneous Tactile Reflexes into Whole-Body Humanoid Control
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents ARC (Ascending Reflex Control), a bottom-up framework that integrates an instantaneous whole-body tactile reflex pathway (delivering withdrawal poses to motors within 10 ms) with learned whole-body control via reflex-in-the-loop learning, reflex-transparent alignment, and reflex-informed adaptation to support sustained withdrawal, balance, and recovery. Deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid and evaluated on three categories of hazardous contact, ARC reduces the first contact force peak by 34.1% and lowers the contact impulse from 0.2632 N·s to 0.1225 N·s (a 2.15× reduction) compared with an otherwise identical reflex delayed by 20 ms. The framework additionally demonstrates protected motion tracking, teleoperation, and vision-free obstacle traversal guided solely by foot tactile sensing, indicating compatibility between fast reflexes and longer-horizon whole-body behaviors.

topic_matches.title: Physical Diffusion Policy via MPM-Guided 3D Gaussian Simulation
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes a physics-aware diffusion policy for robot manipulation that couples 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation to recover object material properties from visual demonstrations using video guidance and particle-level constraints, and then conditions a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy on the estimated physical parameters. To enable practical deployment without online optimization, the method introduces a physics memory bank that retrieves relevant physical conditions, allowing the policy to adapt manipulation behavior across different material regimes without running simulations at test time. Experiments on diverse simulated and real-world objects show that the proposed approach improves manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based policies, suggesting that explicit physical modeling is beneficial for handling heterogeneous object dynamics.

topic_matches.title: Coordinating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Action-Conditioned Latent Foresight
topic_matches.institution: Kinetix AI; Technical University of Munich; The University of Hong Kong; University of Hamburg; University of Science and Technology of China
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model that evaluates proposed humanoid loco-manipulation command sequences via an endpoint predictor of future visual features towards demonstration-derived subgoals and a joint temporal prior enforcing sequence consistency, with execution performed by receding-horizon replanning of the best-scoring sequence. During training, the method uses action consistency regularization to reconstruct the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the latent predictor to preserve action-relevant information for robust sequence evaluation. topic_matches.title: Caging Vision-Language Navigation for Legged Robots via Barrier-Certified Safety Architecture
topic_matches.institution: Toyota Motor Corporation; University of Delaware
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes a safety architecture for legged Vision-Language Navigation that retains a high-level Vision-Language Action planner while adding a low-level physical-grounding layer using state estimation, in-situ 3D spatial perception, and Signed Distance Field representations to generate physically executable trajectories. The navigation planner combines a low-dimensional Bézier-parameterized MPPI scheme with Discrete Exponential Barrier Function constraints to provide provable collision-avoidance guarantees under stated assumptions, effectively “caging” the behavior of end-to-end VLA planners. The modular Legged-VLN system is demonstrated in extensive real-world experiments on humanoid and quadrupedal robots, showing versatile, efficient, and safe language-driven navigation, and is designed to be compatible with different VLM/VLA models and robot platforms.

topic_matches.title: HLO-AMP: Hierarchical Loco-Manipulation from Object-Aware Motion Priors
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes HLO-AMP, a hierarchical loco-manipulation framework in which the low-level controller is trained as an object-aware motion prior via motion imitation on retargeted MoCap of core task primitives with the manipulated object present, thereby capturing natural human-like coordination and realistic distributed contact wrenches while exposing a compact task-space command interface. A reference-free high-level policy is then trained atop the low-level prior, with its action space constrained to the empirical envelope of low-level training data so that it can extend behaviors to long-horizon, multi-stage tasks without issuing off-distribution commands that could destabilize the low-level controller. Instantiated on a Unitree G1 for bimanual box pick-and-place, the resulting single deployed policy generalizes across object masses and dimensions, varying initial and goal poses, and can reactively recover from intentional drops during carrying, indicating robustness to task and payload variations.

topic_matches.title: DexHOT: Learning Hand-Object Configuration Transfer for Dexterous Manipulation
topic_matches.institution: CFCS, School of CS, PKU, China.; National Key Laboratory for Multimedia Information Processing, School of CS, PKU, China.; PrimeBot.; State Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence, BIGAI.
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces DexHOT, which formulates dexterous manipulation as learning a relation-conditioned hand–object configuration transfer primitive that maps between feasible joint hand articulations and object poses relative to the wrist, learned from synthetic feasible configuration pairs without human motion demonstrations. DexHOT composes long-horizon behaviors by closed-loop tracking of sequenced configuration subgoals, using the learned transfer primitive as a reusable building block for complex dexterous tasks. On DexHOTBench with 120 objects, a single DexHOT policy achieves 80.5% transfer success on seen objects and 69.4% on unseen objects; on a real dexterous hand it reaches 61.5% success over 200 transfer trials and 90% task success across six demonstration-guided tasks, indicating that explicit hand–object configuration goals provide an effective control interface.
